newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia economy unlikely to grow in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia economy unlikely to grow in 1997.

text.p: Russia's economy will not grow this year despite government hopes that reforms are finally bringing positive results, but will stabilise and then pick up in 1998, government advisers and officials said on Friday.
"For now we cannot talk of growth, although stabilisation is definitely happening. But next year of course there will be growth," an official at the Economy Ministry said.
Earlier this year Russian officials said 1997 would finally mark an improvement in the economy, which has seen its gross domestic product fall steadily since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Late last month First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said Russia could see 0.5 to 2.5 percent growth this year.
But so far officials can only point to a year-on-year GDP growth of 0.2 percent in the first quarter of this year, a tiny increase analysts say cannot be called real economic growth.
And it seems that even Chubais may be revising his expectations downward.
"The main task of the government must be to ensure that 1998 becomes the year of growth," Chubais told regional governors in the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk this week.
But the State Statistics Committee and some economists say the economy has already turned the corner.

Yevsei Gurvich, an analyst with the Finance Ministry Economic Expert Group, said on Friday that by December GDP growth would be four percent higher than its December 1996 level, although growth would be zero for the year overall.
The group, which makes macroeconomic policy recommendations and forecasts, gave their latest assessment of Russia's economy at a news briefing on Friday.

By the end of 1996 the Russian economy was only 61 percent of its size when the Soviet Union broke up and capitalist reforms began -- shrinking to its size when Leonid Brezhnev led the Kremlin in 1979.

Some analysts have queried the official GDP growth figures, saying the statistics committee increased the weighting given this year to the booming unofficial economy in calculating GDP but left last year's figures unchanged.
Both statistics committee officials and analysts agree that the problems of calculating GDP in the midst of economic upheaval are thorny.

"When the reforms were done nobody thought about needing to reform the statistics system," Misha Belkindas, statistical adviser to the Development Data Group at the World Bank, told a news briefing. "Unfortunately reform of statistics will continue for a very long time."
Statistics Committee officials have said 1996 figures will be revised, however, and that they do not expect the picture of the overall trend to change significantly.
"You cannot attribute the change...in the Russian economy solely to the unofficial economy," said Aleksei Ponomarenko, deputy head of the committee's department for national accounts.
"The main thing is that the trend has changed in the ordinary, official production. The economy is really beginning to come alive."
